Due to a fine cast, some clever dramaturgy and the inherent musical glories of the material, the new Porgy and Bess has integrity.

But that's exactly what makes this Porgy so powerful: It's a show about leaving Catfish Row, about making the great leap from the smothering bosom of the old South into the dark void of the twentieth century.
Despite sugarcoating the tragedy with upbeat promise of redemption, the show respects its internal logic.

In all the design elements, this gutsy new "Porgy" has the glimmer of the ideal solution to forging a show that would honor original intentions, keep Sondheim happy and yet reinvigorate this problematic but masterful piece of theater for a new generation.
Ms. McDonald’s Bess is — in a word — great; the show in which she appears is, at best, just pretty good.
This "Porgy Lite" is not nearly as electrifying as the real thing.
At the same time, there’s little to get excited about: “The Gershwins’ Porgy and Bess,” as it’s now titled, is perfectly adequate — but this Theater production won’t take your breath away.
If you've never seen or heard 'Porgy,' you might well find this version blandly pleasing. Otherwise, you'll be appalled.

So it's a relief to report that the production that opened Thursday at the Theatre is a canny and exuberant re-affirmation of the original's enduring brilliance, neither disrespecting Porgy's creators nor patronizing theatergoers.
The delight in this production is that it seems to move along swiftly as something both new and old - taken on its own terms, as fresh as it is genuine.
She and Lewis make 'Porgy and Bess' a must-see, its flaws notwithstanding.

In the end, though, this is an approachable and heartfelt version of Porgy and Bess that showcases George Gershwin's glorious melodies and the bottomless talents of McDonald.

Seventy-six years after its New York premiere, the great American opera “Porgy and Bess” by George and Ira Gershwin and Dubose and Dorothy Heyward has returned to Broadway in a CliffsNotes edition that is gorgeously sung but conceptually conflicted.
This is a sturdy, at times impressive, version of "Porgy and Bess." But if the goal was to make it a vital drama, that doesn't happen.
Norm Lewis, as Porgy, is the show's saving grace, singing powerfully and playing with a simplicity and quiet intensity that only make McDonald's work seem more artificial.
In all three duets, singing and acting fluidly combine to take you to the heart of the happy-dust-toking, volatile, longing, and feeling Catfish Row crew.

Now that the far-from-happy dust has settled from Stephen Sondheim’s preemptive broadside, now that the Theater production of “The Gershwins’ Porgy and Bess’’ has finally arrived on Broadway, it can be seen, and gloriously heard, for what it is: a fully realized work that pays homage to a classic while infusing it with new, thrilling life.
Certainly the show is a must-see due to Audra McDonald's beautifully sung and fiercely acted portrayal of Bess.
